column2: Seeing it thus turned to ashes, the sons of Pandu, lord, were astonished, O king, and Arjuna said this:
With joined palms, lovingly bowing and saluting: "Govinda, revered one, why has this chariot been burned by fire?
What is this great wonder, delight of the Yadus? Tell me, mighty-armed one, if you think I should hear it."
[Vasudeva said:] "Arjuna, it was burned long ago by many kinds of weapons; because I stood upon it, scorcher of foes, it did not fall to pieces in the battle.
Now it has fallen to pieces, burned by the energy of the Brahma weapon; I let it go, son of Kunti, now that your task is done."
[Sanjaya said:] Smiling a little, the revered Keshava, slayer of foes, embraced King Yudhishthira and said:

By good fortune you have won, son of Kunti; by good fortune your foes are conquered; by good fortune the wielder of Gandiva and Bhimasena, the Pandavas,
mahabharata:9:61.22	are freed from this destruction of heroes, from the battle, their enemies slain. Quickly perform the later duties, Bharata.
mahabharata:9:61.23	At Upaplavya, when you came with the wielder of Gandiva and brought me the madhuparka, what you said to me then:
mahabharata:9:61.24	'This Dhananjaya, Krishna, is your brother and friend, to be protected in all calamities, mighty-armed lord.' As you said so to me, I said, 'So be it.'
mahabharata:9:61.25	That Savyasachin, protected by you, is victorious, lord of men; the brave and truly valiant one, with his brothers, O king of kings, is freed from this destruction of heroes, this hair-raising battle.
Thus addressed by Krishna, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, his hair bristling, replied to Janardana, great king:

The Brahma weapon was loosed by Drona and Karna, crusher of foes.
mahabharata:9:61.28	Who but you could withstand it, even Purandara, wielder of the thunderbolt, in person?
mahabharata:9:61.29	By your grace many were conquered in the battle; Partha, going into the great battle, did not turn away; and likewise, mighty-armed one, by many turns I obtained the continuation of deeds and the auspicious course of splendour.
mahabharata:9:61.30	At Upaplavya the great sage Krishna Dvaipayana told me: 'Where dharma is, there is Krishna; where Krishna is, there is victory.'
When this had been said, those heroes entered your camp, Bharata, and took possession of the treasure, jewels, wealth and stores.
Silver and gold, gems and pearls, choice ornaments, blankets and deerskins, countless male and female slaves and the equipment of kingship.
Obtaining that inexhaustible wealth of yours, bull of the Bharatas, the great archers, conquerors of their foes, shouted aloud, O king.
Those heroes, reassured, unyoked their mounts and rested again and again, all the Pandavas and Satyaki.
Then, great king, the greatly renowned Vasudeva said: "For good fortune we should stay outside the camp."
Saying "So be it," all the Pandavas and Satyaki went outside for good fortune, together with Vasudeva.
Reaching the holy river Oghavati, O king, the Pandavas, their enemies slain, spent that night there.
Then they sent the Yadava to Hastinapura; and mighty Vasudeva, putting Daruka on the chariot, set out swiftly to where the king, son of Ambika, was.
They said to him as he set out, with his chariot yoked to Sainya and Sugriva: "Comfort the renowned Gandhari, whose sons are slain."
Told so by the Pandavas, the best of the Satvatas set out for that city, wishing to reach quickly Gandhari, whose sons were slain.
[Janamejaya said:] "When Krishna went earlier to the Kauravas for peace and did not obtain his wish, then this war took place.
When the warriors were slain and Duryodhana slain, and the Pandava was made free of rivals on earth in battle,
when the camp was fled and empty and supreme fame had been won, what was the reason, Brahmana, for which Krishna went again?
That reason does not seem small to me, Brahmana, that the immeasurable Janardana came himself.
Tell me everything truly, best of Adhvaryus, and what the reason was, Brahmana, in the resolving of this matter."
[Vaishampayana said:] "This question you ask me, O king, is proper for you; I shall tell you it duly, bull of the Bharatas.
Seeing Duryodhana slain by Bhimasena in the battle, mighty son of Dhritarashtra, transgressing the pact, king,
seeing him slain unfairly in the mace-fight, Bharata, great fear entered Yudhishthira, great king.
He thought of the greatly fortunate Gandhari, endowed with austerity; joined to dreadful austerity, she could burn even the three worlds.
As he thought, this idea came to him: that Gandhari, blazing with anger, should first be pacified.
'Hearing of the slaying of her sons, thus done by us, she, enraged, will reduce us to ashes by the fire of her mind.
How will Gandhari bear this keen grief, hearing that her son, who fought straight, was slain by trickery?'
Thinking thus in many ways, filled with fear and grief, the king of dharma said this to Vasudeva:
'By your grace, Govinda, the kingdom without thorns, unattainable even in thought, has been gained by us, Achyuta.
I saw directly, mighty-armed one, that in the hair-raising battle you bore a very great crush, delight of the Yadus.
As you gave aid of old in the war of gods and asuras for the slaying of the enemies of the immortals, and the foes of the gods were slain,
so, mighty-armed one, aid was given to us, Achyuta, and by your charioteering, Vrishni, we were upheld.
If you were not Phalguna's lord in the great battle, how could this ocean of strength have been conquered in the fight?
Mace-blows many, bludgeons too, spears, bhindipalas, tomaras and axes,
and harsh words were borne by you, wishing our good; all these have borne fruit, Achyuta, with Duryodhana slain.
Know, mighty-armed Madhava, the anger of Gandhari; she, greatly fortunate, is ever worn by fierce austerity.
Hearing of the slaying of her sons and grandsons she will surely consume us; I think the time has come to appease her, hero.
Who but you, best of men, could dare to look at her, her eyes blazing with anger, worn by grief for her sons?
It seems right to me that you go there, Madhava, to pacify Gandhari, blazing with anger, subduer of foes.
For you are the maker and unmaker of the worlds, their origin and dissolution; with words joined to reason and cause, urged by Time,
you will pacify Gandhari quickly, greatly wise one; and the revered Krishna (Vyasa) will be there.
In every way, mighty-armed best of the Satvatas, the quenching of Gandhari's anger is to be done by you, well-wisher of the Pandavas.'
Hearing the king of dharma's words, the delight of the Yadu line took leave and said to Daruka, 'Have the chariot made ready.'
Hearing Keshava's words, Daruka hastily announced to the great-souled Keshava that the chariot was ready.
The best of the Yadavas, scorcher of foes, mounting that chariot, went swiftly to Hastinapura, the lord Keshava.
Then, great king, the revered Madhava, the charioteer, reached Nagasahvaya (Hastinapura) and entered, the valiant one.
Entering the city, the hero, making it resound with the rumble of his chariot, known to Dhritarashtra, descended from the best of chariots.
The undismayed one went to Dhritarashtra's dwelling, and there he saw the best of sages (Vyasa) who had arrived before.
Janardana, clasping the feet of Krishna (Vyasa) and then of the king, calmly saluted them, and Keshava also saluted Gandhari.
Then the best of the Yadavas, Adhokshaja, took the king Dhritarashtra by the hand and wept loudly.
After a moment, restraining the tears born of grief, washing his eyes with water and sipping duly, the subduer of foes spoke gentle words to Dhritarashtra:

Nothing is unknown to you of the past and future, Bharata, and the course of Time is well known to you, lord.
mahabharata:9:62.39	How could the destruction of the family and of the kshatriyas not have come about, Bharata, when all the Pandavas followed your wishes?
mahabharata:9:62.40	Having made a pact with his brothers, the dharma-loving one forbore; though capable, cheated at dice, he went to dwell in the forest.
mahabharata:9:62.41	The year lived unknown, wearing various disguises, and many other hardships they bore always as though powerless.
mahabharata:9:62.42	And I myself came when the time of battle was at hand and, in the presence of the whole world, asked you for five villages.
mahabharata:9:62.43	Urged by Time and by greed, you did not give them; through your fault, O king, the whole kshatriya order has perished.
mahabharata:9:62.44	Bhishma, Somadatta, Bahlika, Kripa, Drona with his son, and the wise Vidura constantly begged you for peace, and you did not do it.
mahabharata:9:62.45	All, Bharata, are bewildered when their minds are struck by Time; just as you were deluded earlier in this matter.
mahabharata:9:62.46	What else is there but the conjunction of Time and fate as the final end? Do not lay blame on the Pandavas, great king.
mahabharata:9:62.47	There is not even a small transgression by the great-souled Pandavas, in dharma, in justice or in affection, scorcher of foes.
mahabharata:9:62.48	Knowing all this as the fruit of your own fault, you ought not to harbour resentment against the sons of Pandu.
mahabharata:9:62.49	The family, the line, the offering of funeral cakes and the fruit of sons are today, for you and Gandhari, established in the Pandavas.
mahabharata:9:62.50	Reflecting on all this and on your own transgression, think kindly of the Pandavas; homage to you, bull of the Bharatas.
mahabharata:9:62.51	You know, mighty-armed tiger of the Bharatas, the devotion of the king of dharma to you, and his natural affection as well.
mahabharata:9:62.52	Having done this slaughter of wrongdoing foes, he burns day and night and finds no peace.
mahabharata:9:62.53	Grieving for you, tiger among men, and for the renowned Gandhari, best of the Bharatas, he finds no peace.
mahabharata:9:62.54	Overcome by shame, he does not come to you, afflicted by grief for your sons, your wits and senses bewildered.
Having said this to Dhritarashtra, great king, the best of the Yadus spoke supreme words to Gandhari, worn by grief:

Daughter of Subala, hear what I shall tell you, good vower; there is no woman in this world equal to you today, auspicious one.
mahabharata:9:62.57	I know, queen, how in the assembly in my presence you spoke words joined to dharma and wealth, beneficial to both sides, auspicious one, and your sons did not heed them.
mahabharata:9:62.58	You said harshly to Duryodhana, who sought victory, 'Fool, hear my word: where dharma is, there is victory.'
mahabharata:9:62.59	That word of yours has now come to pass, princess; knowing this, auspicious one, do not set your mind on grief; let your thought never be for the Pandavas' destruction.
mahabharata:9:62.60	You are able, greatly fortunate, by the power of your austerity, to burn up the earth with all that moves and is still with a glance blazing with anger.
Hearing Vasudeva's words, Gandhari said: "It is so, mighty-armed Keshava, as you say.
My mind, burning with grief, had wavered; it has been steadied by hearing your words, Janardana.
For the blind old king whose sons are slain, Keshava, you with those heroic Pandavas are the refuge, best of men."
Having said this much, covering her face with her garment, Gandhari, afflicted with grief for her sons, wept.
Then the mighty-armed lord Keshava consoled the grief-worn woman with words joined to reason and cause.
Having consoled Gandhari and Dhritarashtra, Madhava, Keshava, understood the intention conceived by Drona's son.
Then, hastily rising and bowing his head to the feet of Dvaipayana, O king of kings, he said to the Kaurava:

I take my leave of you, best of the Kurus; do not set your mind on grief. Drona's son has a sinful purpose, and so I have risen suddenly: he has shown his mind to be on the slaying of the Pandavas in the night.
Hearing this, Dhritarashtra, mighty-armed, with Gandhari, said to Keshava, slayer of Keshi:
Go quickly, mighty-armed one, and protect the Pandavas; I shall meet you again soon, Janardana. Then Achyuta set out swiftly with Daruka.
When Vasudeva had gone, king, Vyasa, honoured by the world, the immeasurable one, consoled the king Dhritarashtra.
Vasudeva too, the righteous, his task done, went from Hastinapura to the camp, desiring to see the Pandavas, O king.
Reaching the camp in the night, he went to the Pandavas, told them all that, and entered together with them.
The king was exceedingly wrathful and hostile to the Pandavas; in his supreme calamity what did he say in the great battle?
[Sanjaya said:] "Hear, O king, I shall tell you as it happened, lord of men, what the broken king said when that calamity came.
The king, thighs broken, covered with dust, tying up his hair and looking in the ten directions,
restraining his hair with effort, panting like a serpent, looking at me with eyes full of angry tears,
crushing the ground with his arms again and again like a rutting elephant, shaking his loosened hair, grinding teeth on teeth, reproaching the elder Pandava, sighing, said this:
'With Bhishma son of Shantanu as lord, with Karna, best of weapon-bearers, with Gautama (Kripa), Shakuni and Drona, best of weapon-bearers,
with Ashvatthaman, Shalya and the hero Kritavarman, I have come to this state; Time's course is hard to avoid.
I, master of eleven divisions, have come to this plight; having come to his time, mighty-armed one, none gets past it.
Tell my people, those who yet live in this battle, how I was slain by Bhimasena in transgression of the pact.
Many very cruel deeds were done by the Pandavas against Bhurishravas, Karna, Bhishma and glorious Drona.
And this deed of infamy done by the cruel Pandavas will, I think, cause the good to feel disgust for them.
What joy has one of virtue in a victory won by trickery? What wise man would approve one who breaks a pact?
What wise man would rejoice at a victory won by unrighteousness as the sinful Pandava Vrikodara rejoices?
What wonder is it now that I, thigh-broken, had my head crushed by the foot of enraged Bhimasena?
Whoever treats a man thus, blazing with fortune and abiding among his kin, is surely honoured, Sanjaya.
My mother and father know the dharma of the kshatriyas; they are afflicted with grief; they must be informed in my words, Sanjaya.
I sacrificed, I fed my dependants well, I ruled the earth with her oceans, I stood on the heads of my enemies while they lived, Sanjaya.
I gave gifts as I could, I did what pleased my friends, I oppressed all my enemies—who is more fortunate than I?
I invaded enemy kingdoms, I used kings like slaves, I did good to those dear to me—who is more fortunate than I?
I honoured all my kinsmen, I honoured the worthy and revered them; I served the triple aim—who is more fortunate than I?
I gave commands to chief kings, I obtained honour hard to gain, I rode on the best horses—who is more fortunate than I?
I studied duly, I gave, I attained health and long life, I won worlds by my own dharma—who is more fortunate than I?
By good fortune I was not conquered in battle, did not serve enemies like a servant; by good fortune my great fortune has gone, lord, to another only at my death.
What is desired by kshatriyas who follow their own dharma, this death I have obtained—who is more fortunate than I?
By good fortune I did not turn back from enmity, nor was I conquered like a commoner; by good fortune I was not defeated after taking any thought of surrender.
As one might slay a sleeping or careless man, or by poison, so I was slain, in transgression of dharma and of the pact.
Greatly fortunate Ashvatthaman, Kritavarman the Satvata, and Kripa Sharadvata must be told in my words:
You should not trust the Pandavas, who have acted unrighteously many times and break pacts.'
And your son, truly valiant, said to the weather-seers: 'I was slain in the battle by Bhimasena unrighteously.
I shall follow Drona gone to heaven, Shalya and Karna both, Vrishasena of great valour, Shakuni son of Subala,
Jalasandha of great valour, King Bhagadatta, the great archer Saumadatti, Jayadratha the Sindhu king,
Duhshasana and my other brothers, equal to myself, the valiant Duhshasana's son and my two children Lakshmana,
and these and thousands of my other men; I shall follow behind them like a traveller who has lost his caravan.
How will my sister Dushala, hearing that her brothers and husband are slain, weep, afflicted with grief?
With his daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law, my aged father the king, with Gandhari, crying out, what refuge will he find?
Surely Lakshmana's mother, her sons and lord slain, the auspicious, broad-eyed woman, will soon perish.
If Charvaka, the mendicant skilled in speech, knows of it, that greatly fortunate one will surely avenge me.
At holy Samantapanchaka, renowned in the three worlds, I, meeting my death, shall attain eternal worlds.'
Then thousands of people, filled with tears, hearing the king's lament, fled in the ten directions.
The dreadful earth, with her oceans and forests, moving and unmoving, shook with a roar, and the quarters became turbid.
They reached Drona's son and reported what had happened, the conduct in the mace-fight and the slaying of the king.
Having told that to Drona's son, Bharata, all of them, after reflecting a long time, went away afflicted as they had come.
Pierced by sharp arrows, maces, tomaras and spears, Ashvatthaman, Kripa and Kritavarman the Satvata hastened on swift horses to the battlefield.
There they saw the great-souled son of Dhritarashtra felled, like a great sala tree in the forest broken by the force of the wind.
Rolling on the ground, drenched with blood, like a great elephant in the forest felled by a hunter,
rolling often, flooded with streams of blood, like a sun-disc fallen by chance from the sky,
like an ocean dried up by a great wind, like the full moon in the sky with its orb veiled in mist,
dust-stained, long-armed, with the valour of an elephant, surrounded on every side by dreadful hosts of ghouls and flesh-eaters, like a best of kings surrounded by servants eager for wealth,
his brows knit, his eyes rolling with anger, intolerant, like a tiger among men, like a fallen tiger.
Seeing the king fallen on the ground, all those great archers, Kripa and the other chariot-warriors, were seized with bewilderment.
Descending from their chariots, they ran to the king's side, and seeing Duryodhana, all sat down on the ground.
Then Drona's son, great king, his eyes full of tears, sighing, said to the best of the Bharatas, lord of the lords of the whole world:

Surely nothing is unbearable in human life, if you, tiger among men, lie smeared with dust.
mahabharata:9:64.13	Having been a king, ruling the earth by your commands, how do you lie today, O king of kings, alone in a deserted forest?
mahabharata:9:64.14	I do not see Duhshasana, nor the great chariot-warrior Karna, nor all those friends; what is this, bull of the Bharatas?
mahabharata:9:64.15	It is hard indeed to know the course of the Ender, if you, lord of the worlds, lie smeared with dust.
mahabharata:9:64.16	This one who went at the head of the anointed kings, scorcher of foes, now eats dust with grass; behold the turning of Time.
mahabharata:9:64.17	Where is your spotless parasol, O king, and your fan? Where has that great army of yours gone, best of kings?
mahabharata:9:64.18	The course of events is hard to know through their causes, if you, teacher of the worlds, have come to this plight.
mahabharata:9:64.19	Nothing is lasting among mortals; surely that is seen, looking at the calamity of you who so rivalled Shakra.
Hearing his words, your son, especially grieved, said this fitting word, O king.
Wiping his eyes with his hands, shedding tears born of grief, that lord of men then said to Kripa and all the other heroes:

Such is the law of mortals, declared as ordained by the Creator: the destruction of all beings brought about by the turn of Time.
mahabharata:9:64.23	That has now come to me, before your eyes, who ruled this earth and have reached this end.
mahabharata:9:64.24	By good fortune I did not turn back in battle in any danger; by good fortune I was slain by sinners, and in particular by trickery.
mahabharata:9:64.25	By good fortune I always made effort, eager to fight; by good fortune I am slain in battle with my kinsmen and relatives slain.
mahabharata:9:64.26	By good fortune I see you freed from the destruction of men, in safety and well; that is unsurpassedly dear to me.
mahabharata:9:64.27	Do not grieve over my death, out of friendship; if the Vedas are your authority, I have won imperishable worlds.
mahabharata:9:64.28	Recognising the power of Krishna of immeasurable splendour, I was not made to fall away from the well-practised dharma of the kshatriya.
mahabharata:9:64.29	I have met my end and am in no way to be pitied; you have done what befits yourselves; we always strove for victory, but fate is hard to overcome.
Having said this much, his eyes dim with tears, the king fell silent, overcome with pain.
Seeing the king so, filled with tears and grief, Drona's son blazed with anger like fire at the dissolution of the world.
The Pandavas, victorious, strong, eager, with their aims achieved, strikers, cannot be slain by me today; and their slaying was vowed by me in the king's presence.
Slain, one gains heaven; slaying, one gains fame; both are of great merit to us; there is no fruitlessness in battle.
It is so, mighty-armed Bharata, as you say; there was nothing that Karna and Arjuna could not bear in battle.
[The serpent said:] "I was impelled by Time and impelled you to be a serpent; neither you nor I am the cause of this child's destruction."
Asuras and gods, for the sake of merit, undertake the rite of sacrifice; therefore sacrifices are the final refuge.
Whatever sin the sons of Dhritarashtra had done before, the king (Yudhishthira) did not hold it in his heart and followed that king.
Reflecting on that time, Janardana, slayer of Keshi, considered that the thirty-sixth year had come.
As all those followers of yoga went swiftly, Draupadi, her yoga failing, fell to the ground.
With severed arms, thighs and hands smeared with fat and blood, with cut bellies and feet, scattered here and there.
